claim: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women.
source: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of death in women (Edwards et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2014

claim: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of death in women.
source: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of death in women (Edwards et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2014

claim: About 75% of breast cancers express estrogen receptor alpha (ERα).
source: About 75% of breast cancers express estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), a hormone-regulated transcription factor (Dunnwald et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunnwald et al., 2007

claim: ERα is a hormone-regulated transcription factor.
source: About 75% of breast cancers express estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), a hormone-regulated transcription factor (Dunnwald et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunnwald et al., 2007 and established scientific knowledge

claim: ERα-positive breast cancers typically respond well to therapy that attenuates ERα signaling.
source: ERα-positive breast cancers typically respond well to therapy that attenuates ERα signaling, either by blocking the production of estrogens via aromatase inhibitors, or antagonizing the activity of estrogens through competitive binding of ER antagonists such as tamoxifen (Puhalla et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puhalla et al., 2012

claim: Patients frequently relapse after prolonged endocrine therapy.
source: While estrogen disrupting therapies are often effective both in the adjuvant and metastatic setting, patients frequently relapse after prolonged therapy (Chia et al., 2008; Dowsett et al., 2010; Davies et al., 2011; Mauri et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Chia et al., 2008; Dowsett et al., 2010; Davies et al., 2011; Mauri et al., 2006

claim: Relapsed tumors remain dependent on ER.
source: Though resistance to endocrine therapies frequently emerges, relapsed tumors remain dependent on ER, which is highlighted by patient responses to second and third line endocrine therapies after failure of an earlier line (Mouridsen et al., 2009; Howell et al., 2005; Lewis and Jordan, 2005; Perey et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Mouridsen et al., 2009; Howell et al., 2005; Lewis and Jordan, 2005; Perey et al., 2007

claim: ESR1 mutations in the ligand binding domain are found at high prevalence (25–40%) in relapsed, metastatic patients.
source: More recently however, a series of mutations in the ligand binding domain of ERα have been found at a high prevalence (25–40%) in relapsed, metastatic patients, though are very rare in untreated populations (Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013

claim: ESR1 mutations are very rare in untreated populations.
source: More recently however, a series of mutations in the ligand binding domain of ERα have been found at a high prevalence (25–40%) in relapsed, metastatic patients, though are very rare in untreated populations (Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013

claim: ESR1 mutations confer estrogen-independent activity to the receptor in overexpression experiments.
source: These mutations have been shown in overexpression experiments to confer estrogen-independent activity to the receptor, and to reduce the potency of, for example, tamoxifen.
evidence: Supported by citations in the preceding sentence: Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013

claim: ESR1 mutations reduce the potency of tamoxifen.
source: These mutations have been shown in overexpression experiments to confer estrogen-independent activity to the receptor, and to reduce the potency of, for example, tamoxifen.
evidence: Supported by citations in the preceding sentence: Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013

claim: SERDs are competitive ERα antagonists that induce ubiquitination and degradation of ERα via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Selective ER Downregulators (SERDs) are competitive ERα antagonists that also induce a conformational shift of the receptor that results in ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of ERα, via the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Berry et al., 2008; Wijayaratne and McDonnell, 2001; Wijayaratne et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations: Berry et al., 2008; Wijayaratne and McDonnell, 2001; Wijayaratne et al., 1999

claim: Fulvestrant has clinical impact as a treatment of recurrent, endocrine resistant disease.
source: Indeed, the clinical impact of fulvestrant as a treatment of recurrent, endocrine resistant disease, supports this notion (Perey et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perey et al., 2007

claim: Fulvestrant is limited by poor pharmaceutical properties that necessitate administration by intramuscular injection.
source: Though fulvestrant has served as an important proof of concept for the SERD approach [see also (Ellis et al., 2015)], it is limited by its poor pharmaceutical properties, which necessitates administration by intramuscular injection and limits the applied dose, exposure, and receptor engagement (Robertson et al., 2001; van Kruchten et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations: Robertson et al., 2001; van Kruchten et al., 2015

claim: The fulvestrant 500 mg regimen exhibited improvement in progression free survival and overall survival over the 250 mg regimen.
source: The fulvestrant 500 mg regimen (500 mg on day 1, 14, 28; monthly thereafter) exhibited improvement in progression free survival and overall survival over the initially approved and marketed 250 mg regimen (Di Leo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Leo et al., 2010

claim: The fulvestrant 500 mg dose does not fully saturate ER binding in patients.
source: However, the 500 mg dose does not fully saturate ER binding in patients, as inhibition of [18F]fluoroestradiol uptake was incomplete in 38% (6/16) of patients analyzed.
evidence: Supported by data from van Kruchten et al., 2015 cited in the preceding sentence

claim: Lack of receptor occupancy by fulvestrant was associated with lack of clinical benefit.
source: Importantly, this lack of receptor occupancy was associated with lack of clinical benefit (van Kruchten et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Kruchten et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 is a novel, non-steroidal, orally bioavailable selective ER downregulator (SERD).
source: Here we describe GDC-0810, a novel, non-steroidal, orally bioavailable selective ER downregulator (SERD), which was identified by prospectively optimizing ERα degradation, antagonism and pharmacokinetic properties.
evidence: Supported by data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: GDC-0810 was identified by prospectively optimizing ERα degradation, antagonism and pharmacokinetic properties.
source: Here we describe GDC-0810, a novel, non-steroidal, orally bioavailable selective ER downregulator (SERD), which was identified by prospectively optimizing ERα degradation, antagonism and pharmacokinetic properties.
evidence: Supported by data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: GDC-0810 induces a distinct ERα conformation relative to currently approved therapeutics.
source: GDC-0810 induces a distinct ERα conformation, relative to that induced by currently approved therapeutics, suggesting a unique mechanism of action.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A showing conformational profiling

claim: GDC-0810 has robust in vitro and in vivo activity against a variety of human breast cancer cell lines and patient derived xenografts.
source: GDC-0810 has robust in vitro and in vivo activity against a variety of human breast cancer cell lines and patient derived xenografts, including a tamoxifen-resistant model and those that harbor ERα mutations.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figures 4-8

claim: GDC-0810 has activity against tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer models.
source: GDC-0810 has robust in vitro and in vivo activity against a variety of human breast cancer cell lines and patient derived xenografts, including a tamoxifen-resistant model and those that harbor ERα mutations.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5

claim: GDC-0810 has activity against breast cancer models that harbor ERα mutations.
source: GDC-0810 has robust in vitro and in vivo activity against a variety of human breast cancer cell lines and patient derived xenografts, including a tamoxifen-resistant model and those that harbor ERα mutations.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 6-8

claim: GDC-0810 is currently being evaluated in Phase II clinical studies in women with ER+ breast cancer.
source: GDC-0810 is currently being evaluated in Phase II clinical studies in women with ER+ breast cancer.
evidence: Statement about ongoing clinical trials

claim: GDC-0810 reduces cellular ERα levels within 4 hr with sub-nanomolar potency.
source: GDC-0810 was prioritized for further characterization based on its ability to robustly reduce cellular ERα levels within 4 hr, to levels approaching that observed with fulvestrant, with sub-nanomolar potency (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1B and Table 1

claim: 4-hydroxytamoxifen exhibits some activity in reducing ERα signal but fails to reduce ERα to the level achieved by fulvestrant or GDC-0810.
source: The active metabolite of tamoxifen, 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4OH-tamoxifen), exhibited some activity in this assay, though it failed to reduce ERα signal to the level achieved by fulvestrant or GDC-0810.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1B

claim: GDC-0810-mediated ERα depletion is dependent on the 26S proteasome.
source: We further demonstrated that GDC-0810-mediated ERα depletion is dependent on the 26S proteasome, since addition of the proteasome inhibitor MG132, fully blocked GDC-0810 depletion of ERα, similar to the effect of MG132 treatment in preventing fulvestrant-mediated ER turnover (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1C,D showing MG132 blocks ERα depletion

claim: GDC-0810 binds both ERα and ERβ with low nanomolar affinity.
source: In cell-free radio-ligand competitive binding assays, GDC-0810 binds both ERα and ERβ with low nanomolar affinity [Table 1, see also (Lai et al., 2015)].
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 and citation to Lai et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 effectively antagonizes E2-mediated transcriptional activation of an ER reporter construct in MCF7 cells with nanomolar potency.
source: In MCF7 cells GDC-0810 effectively antagonizes E2-mediated transcriptional activation of an ER reporter construct and inhibits cell proliferation with nanomolar potency and efficacy similar to that of fulvestrant and 4OH-tamoxifen (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: GDC-0810 inhibits MCF7 cell proliferation with nanomolar potency and efficacy similar to fulvestrant and 4OH-tamoxifen.
source: In MCF7 cells GDC-0810 effectively antagonizes E2-mediated transcriptional activation of an ER reporter construct and inhibits cell proliferation with nanomolar potency and efficacy similar to that of fulvestrant and 4OH-tamoxifen (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: GDC-0810 is selective against other nuclear hormone receptor (NHR) family members.
source: GDC-0810 is selective against the other nuclear hormone receptor (NHR) family members as monitored by competitive binding and reporter activation assays (Supplementary file 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1A-C

claim: The GDC-0810:ER complex recruits a distinct set of peptides relative to other ER:ligand complexes.
source: The GDC-0810:ER complex recruits a distinct set of peptides relative to the other ER:ligand complexes profiled here, with the exception of GW7604 (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A and citation to Lai et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 induces an ER conformational profile that is different from that induced by 4OH-tamoxifen, fulvestrant and other marketed SERMs and similar to GW7604.
source: GDC-0810 thus induces an ER conformational profile that is different from that induced by 4OH-tamoxifen, fulvestrant and other marketed SERMs and similar to GW7604 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A

claim: GDC-0810 displays little of the transcriptional agonist activity observed with SERMs in MCF7 cells in the absence of estrogen.
source: GDC-0810 most closely resembled fulvestrant and GW7604 in this analysis, displaying little of the transcriptional agonist activity observed with the SERMs 4OH-tamoxifen, lasofoxifene, arzoxifene or endoxifene and often demonstrating inverse agonist activity on estradiol responsive genes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2B

claim: GDC-0810 treatment reduces the levels of ERα associated with chromatin on ERα target genes.
source: These findings are consistent with ER-ChIP analysis demonstrating that GDC-0810 treatment, similar to fulvestrant, can reduce the levels of ERα associated with chromatin on ERα target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: GDC-0810 can inhibit ER signaling in the absence of ER degradation.
source: These data imply that GDC-0810 has the ability to antagonize ER function independent from its degradation activity, consistent with the demonstration that GDC-0810 displaces the co-activator PGC1α in cell free biochemical assays, in which ER degradation does not occur (see below, Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2C-E and Figure 6A

claim: GDC-0810 modestly increases alkaline phosphatase activity in Ishikawa endometrial cells.
source: GDC-0810 modestly increases alkaline phosphatase activity, though plateaus at low concentrations, below the level stimulated by 4OH-tamoxifen (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3A

claim: GDC-0810 at 0.1 or 10 mg/kg did not significantly alter uterine wet weight relative to vehicle control in juvenile rats.
source: GDC-0810 dosed at 0.1 or 10 mg/kg did not significantly alter uterine wet relative to the vehicle control (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3B

claim: GDC-0810 induced a cuboidal to columnar morphological change in the endometrial epithelial cells in juvenile rats.
source: Importantly though, histological analysis and quantification of endometrial cell height showed that, like estradiol and tamoxifen, GDC-0810 induced a cuboidal to columnar morphological change in the epithelial cells, while the epithelia from fulvestrant-treated animals remained cuboidal (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3C,D

claim: GDC-0810 induces ER target genes in the rat uterus.
source: In line with the observed morphological changes to the endometrial epithelium, gene expression analysis demonstrated that GDC-0810 induces ER target genes, including C3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3E

claim: GDC-0810 only modestly reduces ER levels in the rat uterus.
source: Intriguingly, IHC analysis of ER in the uterus showed that GDC-0810 only modestly reduces ER levels in this context, similar to estradiol, while fulvestrant robustly depletes ER.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3C,F

claim: GDC-0810 exhibits low clearance (11 mL/min/kg) and 61% oral bioavailability in mice.
source: In mice, GDC-0810 exhibits low clearance (11 mL/min/kg) and 61% oral bioavailability (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 plasma concentrations increase proportionately with the applied dose in mice.
source: Importantly, GDC-0810 plasma concentrations increase proportionately with the applied dose and achieve an AUC0–24 of 94.1 μg*hr/ml when dosed by oral gavage at 100 mg/kg/day (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2A

claim: GDC-0810 displayed dose dependent efficacy in the MCF7 xenograft model.
source: In the MCF7 xenograft model, GDC-0810 displayed dose dependent efficacy (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A

claim: GDC-0810 at 100 mg/kg/day caused tumor regressions in MCF7 xenografts.
source: The 100 mg/kg/day dose caused tumor regressions; an effect similar to withdrawal of estrogen pellets at the start of dosing.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A

claim: Fulvestrant at a clinically relevant dose yielded only modest tumor growth inhibition in MCF7 xenografts.
source: In contrast, fulvestrant, at a clinically relevant dose as well as at a considerably higher dose (200 mg/kg, 3 times per week), yielded only modest tumor growth inhibition (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: GDC-0810 at 100 mg/kg/day robustly modulated ER target genes in MCF7 tumors.
source: Gene expression analysis of harvested MCF7 tumors demonstrated that GDC-0810 (at 100 mg/kg/day, evaluated on day 28) robustly modulated ER target genes, including PGR, c-MYC, AREG and MUC1 (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: GDC-0810 at 10 mg/kg/day and 100 mg/kg/day reduced FES uptake by 45 and 63 percent respectively in MCF7 xenografts.
source: However, when assayed after the seventh consecutive oral daily dose, GDC-0810 at 10 mg/kg/day and 100 mg/kg/day reduced FES uptake by 45 and 63 percent respectively (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4D,E

claim: GDC-0810 dosed at 10 and 100 mg/kg/day drove tumor stasis in the HCI-003 PDX model.
source: GDC-0810, dosed at 10 and 100 mg/kg/day in mice implanted with 1 mg E2 impregnated beeswax pellets, drove tumor stasis, while fulvestrant dosed at 30 times the clinical exposure induced tumor regression, approaching that observed in vehicle treated animals whose estradiol pellets were excised at start of the dosing period (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4F

claim: GDC-0810 treated HCI-003 tumors displayed reduced ERα target gene transcription and reduced ERα protein levels.
source: Consistent with GDC-0810 SERD activity in vitro, tumors collected after 43 days of dosing displayed reduced ERα target gene transcription and reduced ERα protein levels, as monitored by quantitative PCR and Western Blot, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: GDC-0810 displayed anti-tumor activity in ZR75-1, an ER+ breast cancer xenograft model.
source: GDC-0810 also displayed anti-tumor activity in ZR75-1, an additional ER+ breast cancer xenograft model (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: GDC-0810 did not exhibit any anti-tumor activity in MDA-MB-231, an ER negative human breast cancer tumor model.
source: Importantly, GDC-0810 did not exhibit any anti-tumor activity in MDA-MB-231, an ER negative human breast cancer tumor model (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Treatment of TamR1 xenografts with tamoxifen stimulated tumor growth relative to E2 pellet harboring vehicle controls.
source: Consistent with other reported xenograft models of tamoxifen resistance, treatment of the TamR1 xenografts with tamoxifen stimulated tumor growth, relative to the E2 pellet harboring vehicle controls [Figure 5A, and (Connor et al., 2001; Gottardis and Jordan, 1988; Lai et al., 2015)].
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5A and citations: Connor et al., 2001; Gottardis and Jordan, 1988; Lai et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 induced regression at all doses tested (10, 30, 100 mg/kg/day) in TamR1 tumors grown with 0.18 mg E2 pellets.
source: In TamR1 tumors grown under these conditions of lower E2, GDC-0810 induced regression at all doses tested (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5A

claim: GDC-0810 treatment resulted in a dramatic reduction in ERα levels in TamR1 xenograft tumors by immunohistochemistry and Western blot.
source: Similar to the in vitro observations, GDC-0810 treatment resulted in a dramatic reduction in ERα levels in the xenograft tumors by both immunohistochemistry and Western blot (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: GDC-0810 treated TamR1 tumors display reduced Ki-67 staining.
source: Consistent with the anti-tumor effect, GDC-0810 treated tumors display reduced Ki-67 staining (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and altered ER target gene transcription in a manner consistent with ER antagonism (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: GDC-0810 retains its ability to potently displace E2 from the ligand binding domain of ER.Y537S and ER.D538G mutants, albeit with a slightly increased IC50.
source: In cell-free E2 competitive binding assays, GDC-0810 retains its ability to potently displace E2 from the ligand binding domain, albeit with a slightly increased IC50 (WT: 2.6 nM vs. ER.Y537S: 5.5 nM and ER.D538G: 5.4 nM) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6A

claim: GDC-0810 can compete the PGC1α co-activator peptide off the mutated ligand binding domain with ~five–seven fold reduction in biochemical potency compared to wild-type ER.
source: We next determined that GDC-0810 can compete the PGC1α co-activator peptide off the mutated ligand binding domain, implying that GDC-0810 is capable of driving an 'active' to 'inactive' conformational shift of mutant ER, though with a ~five–seven fold reduction in biochemical potency compared to wild-type ER (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6B

claim: MCF7 ER.Y537S cells display a high level of estrogen-independent ER pathway activity.
source: Despite expressing only 33% mutant RNA, ER.Y537S cells display a high level of estrogen-independent ER pathway activity, as demonstrated by high expression of the ER-target genes, TFF1, GREB1 and PGR, in the absence of estrogen, although these genes can be further stimulated with the addition of estrogen (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6C

claim: GDC-0810 displays a marked reduction in potency in ER.Y537S versus ER.WT cells in the absence of E2.
source: When the viability assay is conducted in the absence of E2, GDC-0810 displays a marked reduction in potency in the mutant versus wild-type setting, with 22 fold higher concentration being required to achieve 50% maximal inhibition of growth in the ER.Y537S versus ER.WT cells (Figure 6D, solid black line vs. solid blue line).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6D

claim: GDC-0810 reduces steady-state levels of ER protein in both ER.WT and ER.Y537S cells.
source: GDC-0810 reduces steady-state levels of ER protein, in both ER.WT and ER.Y537S cells, demonstrating that the presence of ER.Y537S does not preclude GDC-0810-mediated ER-degradation, though due to a mixed population of ER.WT and ER.Y537S we cannot directly determine if GDC-0810 induced degradation of ER.Y537S is any more or less efficient than that of ER.WT (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6E

claim: GDC-0810 reduces both estrogen-driven and mutant-driven PR protein levels.
source: GDC-0810 reduces both estrogen-driven, and mutant-driven PR protein levels, athough residual PR is still detected in the mutant cells at 24 hr post compound addition (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6E

claim: T47D ER.D538G cells express endogenous levels of total ER but very high levels of PR relative to WT cells, even in the absence of estrogen.
source: T47D ER.D538G cells, expressing WT:D538G mRNA at a 1:1 ratio (data not shown) express endogenous levels of total ER, though very high levels of PR relative to WT cells, even in the absence of estrogen, implying robust estrogen-independent pathway activity (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7A

claim: GDC-0810 suppresses the proliferation of both T47D ER.WT cells and ER.D538G cells with modest differences in potency.
source: In cell viability assays, GDC-0810 suppresses the proliferation of both ER.WT cells and ER.D538G cells, with modest differences in potency (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7B

claim: T47D ER.D538G cells robustly outcompete ER.WT cells when grown in the absence of estrogen.
source: When mixed at a 1:1 ratio at day 0, and grown in the absence of estrogen, ER.D538G cells robustly outcompete ER.WT cells, with WT cells representing only 7.8% (± 1%) of the total population on day 15 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7C,D

claim: In the presence of 0.1 nM estrogen, much of the competitive advantage of T47D ER.D538G cells over ER.WT cells is lost.
source: In the presence of 0.1 nM estrogen however, much of this competitive advantage is lost, with WT cells representing 40% ± 0.2% of the total population at day 15 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7C,D

claim: GDC-0810 attenuates both the estrogen-dependent growth of T47D ER.WT cells and estrogen-independent growth of ER.D538G cells.
source: GDC-0810 attenuates both the estrogen-dependent growth of ER.WT cells, as well as estrogen-independent growth of the ER.D538G cells, though both cell types continue to proliferate at low levels in the presence of drug.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7C,D

claim: ER mutant cells do not confer a non-cell autonomous growth signal to ER.WT cells grown in the absence of estrogen.
source: These cell labeling/cell competition experiments further indicate that ER mutant cells do not confer a non-cell autonomous growth signal to ER.WT cells grown in the absence of estrogen, since ER.WT cells grow at the same rate, regardless of whether they are grown alone, or co-cultured with estrogen-independent ER.D538G cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7E

claim: GDC-0810 100 mg/kg/day p.o. induced tumor regressions in the HA-ER.Y537S overexpressing model.
source: Strikingly, GDC-0810 100 mg/kg/day p.o. induced tumor regressions in the HA-ER.Y537S overexpressing model, while tamoxifen 60 mg/kg/day p.o. and fulvestrant 200 mg/kg SC (3x/week) resulted in tumor stasis at exposures higher than those achieved in clinic (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8A

claim: GDC-0810 dosed orally at 100 mg/kg and fulvestrant dosed intramuscularly at 200 mg/kg for 4 days both modulate ER regulated targets in WHIM20 PDX.
source: A pharmacodynamic (PD) experiment showed that GDC-0810, dosed orally at 100 mg/kg, and fulvestrant dosed intramuscularly at the high dose of 200 mg/kg for 4 days, both modulate a collection of known ER regulated targets, including robust suppression of RASGRP1 and AREG, as examples (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8B

claim: GDC-0810 and fulvestrant treatment resulted in modest decreases in ER and PR protein levels in WHIM20 PDX.
source: Western blot analysis, quantitative reverse phase protein array (RPPA) and IHC of ER and PR, in the same 4-day PD experiment, demonstrated that GDC-0810 and fulvestrant treatment resulted in modest decreases in ER and PR protein levels (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8C,D

claim: GDC-0810 100 mg/kg/day treatment and tamoxifen 60 mg/kg/day induced tumor stasis in WHIM20 PDX.
source: Importantly, in a separate efficacy study, GDC-0810 100 mg/kg/day treatment and tamoxifen 60 mg/kg/day induced tumor stasis, while fulvestrant at at a dose that roughly achieves plasma levels similar to those achieved with the 500-mg dose in humans (50 mg/kg days 1, 3 and 7, 25 mg/kg weekly thereafter; 0.015 mg/mL at trough on day 21, AUC ~0.36 μg*hr/mL) did not induce regression but resulted in tumor growth inhibition (Figure 8E, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8E and Supplementary file 2B

claim: Complete/near complete (>90%) suppression of FES uptake was observed in 90% of patients with FES-PET scans in the Phase I dose escalation study of GDC-0810.
source: In the Phase I dose escalation study in postmenopausal women with ER+ locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer (clinicaltrials.gov NCT01823835), complete/near complete (>90%) suppression of FES uptake was reported to be observed in 90% of patients with FES-PET scans, including 5 patients with known ESR1 mutations, providing early clinical evidence of robust ER engagement by GDC-0810 [(Dickler et al., 2015), and manuscript in preparation].
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickler et al., 2015 and reference to manuscript in preparation

claim: ESR1 mutations in plasma DNA predict relative resistance to AIs but not to fulvestrant.
source: These data are consistent with recent retrospective clinical studies showing that ESR1 mutations in plasma DNA predict relative resistance to AIs but not to fulvestrant (Fribbens et al., 2016; Schiavon et al., 2015; Spoerke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations: Fribbens et al., 2016; Schiavon et al., 2015; Spoerke et al., 2016

claim: The Y537S and D538G substitutions shift ER into a conformation that resembles an active/liganded ER wild-type conformation.
source: Structural studies and molecular dynamics simulations of ER mutants have demonstrated that the Y537S and D538G substitutions shift ER, and particularly helix 12 (H12), into a conformation that resembles an active/liganded ER wild-type conformation, providing a molecular explanation for the constitutive activity of these mutations (Nettles et al., 2008; Toy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations: Nettles et al., 2008; Toy et al., 2013

claim: The 'pre-organized agonist state' of ER mutants restricts access to the ligand binding domain, which influences binding of both estrogen and tamoxifen.
source: A recent biophysical analysis of these mutants has provided an important extension of those findings, demonstrating that this 'pre-organized agonist state' restricts access to the ligand binding domain, which influences binding of both estrogen and tamoxifen, and presumably other ligands, including GDC-0810, which is consistent with what we show here (Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fanning et al., 2016

claim: Tamoxifen fails to fully restore H12 as well as the H11-12 loop back to the wild-type antagonist state in ER mutants.
source: Fanning et al. further demonstrate that tamoxifen fails to fully restore H12 as well as the H11-12 loop back to the wild-type antagonist state, providing a further explanation for reduced tamoxifen potency in the mutant context.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fanning et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence

claim: GDC-0810 is a product of efforts to capitalize on the advantages associated with the SERD approach while overcoming the limitations associated with fulvestrant.
source: However, pre-clinical and clinical data indicate that fulvestrant's therapeutic action is limited by its poor pharmaceutical properties. GDC-0810 is a product of efforts to capitalize on the advantages associated with the SERD approach, while overcoming the limitations associated with fulvestrant.
evidence: Supported by data throughout the manuscript

claim: GDC-0810 is a non-steroidal, orally bioavailable dual function ER antagonist and down-regulator that induces potent, rapid proteasome-mediated ERα degradation in breast cancer cells.
source: GDC-0810 is a non-steroidal, orally bioavailable dual function ER antagonist and down-regulator that induces potent, rapid proteasome-mediated ERα degradation in breast cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 1-3

claim: GDC-0810 binds ERα with low nanomolar potency.
source: GDC-0810 binds ERα with low nanomolar potency, exhibits good oral bioavailability, and dose-dependent/linear pharmacokinetics in the mouse.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 and Supplementary file 2A

claim: GDC-0810 exhibits good oral bioavailability and dose-dependent/linear pharmacokinetics in the mouse.
source: GDC-0810 binds ERα with low nanomolar potency, exhibits good oral bioavailability, and dose-dependent/linear pharmacokinetics in the mouse.
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2A and citation to Lai et al., 2015

claim: GDC-0810 displays robust anti-tumor activity in cell line-based and patient derived xenograft models of breast cancer when administered orally once daily at well-tolerated doses.
source: When administered orally, once daily, at doses that deliver substantial plasma concentrations and are well-tolerated, GDC-0810 displays robust anti-tumor activity in cell line-based and patient derived xenograft models of breast cancer.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 4-8

claim: The GDC-0810:ER complex interacts with a set of peptides that are distinct from those that interact with the fulvestrant:ER complex.
source: Though GDC-0810 clearly shares features with fulvestrant, such as the ability to down-regulate ER protein levels in breast cancer cells, the GDC-0810:ER complex interacts with a set of peptides that are distinct from those that interact with the fulvestrant:ER complex, suggesting that these compounds promote distinct ER conformations, and may therefore have a different mechanism by which they induce ER turnover.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A

claim: GDC-0810 and fulvestrant have distinct mechanisms by which they induce ER degradation.
source: The observations that 1) saturation of the GDC-0810 and the fulvestrant ER degradation machinery occur differentially in our doxycycline-inducible ER-over-expressing MCF7 cell line (Figure 2C) and 2) that fulvestrant, but not GDC-0810, drives degradation of ER in the rat uterus (Figure 3C,F), further supports the notion that these compounds have distinct mechanisms by which they induce ER degradation, and potentially require differing co-factors or distinct sets of E3 ligases.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 2C and Figure 3C,F

claim: ER degradation may be associated with preventing ER agonism in the rat uterus.
source: The observation that activation of the ER pathway occurs concomitantly with lack of robust ER degradation upon GDC-0810 treatment in the rat uterus suggests that although ER degradation is not absolutely required for direct ER antagonism, it may be associated with preventing ER agonism, at least in this context.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 3

claim: The binding of the GW5P2 and 47P3 peptides to the ER:GDC-0810 complex likely reflects the presence of an acrylic acid side chain in GDC-0810.
source: Notably, the binding of the GW5P2 and 47P3 peptides to various ER:ligand complexes was highly correlated with the presence of an acrylic or carboxylic acid head group in ligand structures (Iannone et al., 2004). The binding of GW5P2 and 47P3 to the ER:GDC-0810 complex thus likely reflects the presence of this acrylic acid side chain in GDC-0810.
evidence: Supported by citation to Iannone et al., 2004 and inference from chemical structure

claim: GDC-0810 mildly stimulates ER signaling in the uterus, similar to the recently described SERD AZD9496.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that GDC-0810 mildly stimulates ER signaling in the uterus, similar to the recently described SERD AZD9496 (Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3 and citation to Weir et al., 2016

claim: The benefit of SERDs vs. non-degrader antagonists will be most apparent in contexts where ER becomes reactivated in the presence of drug.
source: We argue that the benefit of SERDs vs. non-degrader antagonists will be most apparent in those contexts where ER becomes reactivated in the presence of drug, such as is observed in the TamR1 xenograft, in which tamoxifen behaves as a strong agonist.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on data in Figure 5
